beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Intro to Explorer and O O D. The web front door to the Explorer cluster: launch apps, move files and start jobs from a browser, with no terminal required.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Hola. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. Explorer is not a big computer where you run your code. It's a cluster of computers, and you ask it for a slice. This lecture is the whole introduction: what a cluster is, how you get an account, how you log in through the terminal or the Open OnDemand website, where your files live, how you move data, how you run and check a job, how to right-size it, and how software works.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. An HPC cluster: many computers wired together to work on one problem. A login node: the machine you land on, for light work only. A compute node: a machine that does the heavy work, handed to you on request. Slurm: the scheduler that takes those requests and decides who runs where. A partition: a named group of nodes with its own limits. And Open OnDemand, OOD: a website that gives you the cluster in a browser.

beats.narration_text: Start with the shape of the thing. A cluster is many computers working together on problems too big for one desk. You log in to a login node. Light work happens there: editing a file, looking around. When you need real computing power, the work moves to a compute node, and a scheduler called Slurm manages everyone's requests for those nodes.

beats.narration_text: Explorer is Northeastern's cluster, run by the Research Computing team, and it replaced the older Discovery cluster. Forty-five thousand CPU cores. More than five hundred twenty-five GPUs. Free of charge to every Northeastern faculty member and student. It lives at the Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center in Holyoke.

shot.visual_intent: Two counters climb: '45,000' over a grid of CPU squares, '525+' over a smaller grid of dark GPU squares; a small 'Holyoke, MA' label lands beside a building block; 'free' lands as a tag.

beats.narration_text: Around the compute: a ten-gigabit link to the university network for moving data in and out, six petabytes of fast shared storage, and between the nodes themselves either ten-gigabit ethernet or InfiniBand at one or two hundred gigabits a second, so every size of workload has a place.

beats.narration_text: Getting on. For research, every user belongs to a storage space owned by a PI or staff member; storage is free up to thirty-five terabytes. If your lab has one, the PI adds you with the project command, or you file an access request. If it doesn't, the PI requests a storage space first. For coursework, your instructor applies through the classroom access form, and students get in through the course.

beats.narration_text: Two ways in. The terminal, and the Open OnDemand website. Both reach the same cluster. The team's advice is to get comfortable with the terminal, and we'll use both.

beats.narration_text: From a Mac, open Terminal and s s h to login dot explorer dot northeastern dot e d u with your Northeastern username. It asks for your password; the cursor doesn't move while you type it, which is normal. The welcome banner means you're on. On Windows, install an SSH client such as MobaXterm or PuTTY and point it at the same host, port twenty-two.

beats.narration_text: Now, where things live. Everyone has a home directory and a scratch directory. Researchers also have a projects space. Students in a course have a courses space, and may not have projects. Always write the full path, starting with a slash, so a script means the same place wherever it runs.

beats.narration_text: Each has a size. Home holds seventy-five gigabytes, and it fills fastest; when it does, you'll see quota exceeded. Scratch holds fifty terabytes, but it's purged on the first Tuesday of every month, so it's no place for anything you want to keep. Projects is the long-term home for big data and for folders of many small files. A course space holds one to five terabytes, shared by the whole class.

beats.narration_text: Paths in practice. L S lists a directory, and cat prints a file. With an absolute path you can read any file you have permission for, from anywhere on the cluster.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Moving data in. From your own machine, S C P copies a file to the cluster through the transfer node. Make a small test file, copy it into your home directory, then log in and l s to see it arrive. To put it in your project space instead, change the destination path. Many small files? Zip or tar them first.

beats.narration_text: Or use the website. On the Open OnDemand dashboard, open Files, then Home Directory. The Files app starts in your home directory, and the Change directory button takes you to scratch or projects.

beats.narration_text: Upload opens a window where you browse for files or drop them in. The Files app is limited to ten gigabytes a transfer. Bigger than that, use S C P; for very large datasets, Globus. And the same app downloads files, edits them, and makes new folders.

beats.narration_text: Running jobs. So far we've only used the login nodes and the transfer node. Real computation has to move to a compute node: no scientific software, big transfers or heavy work on the login node, because its traffic slows the whole cluster for everyone.

beats.narration_text: From the terminal, s run gets you a compute node. The simplest form takes the defaults: four hours, one node, one task, two gigabytes of memory, two CPUs, on the short partition. Flags ask for more: here, six hours, fifty gigabytes, sixteen tasks. Every flag has a short form too.

props.title: ssh — login.explorer.northeastern.edu
lines: # defaults: 4 h, 1 node, 1 task, 2 GB, 2 CPUs, partition short

beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: A partition is how the team groups nodes: by time limit, by node count, by CPU or GPU. On Explorer: short, the default, and sharing for CPU work. gpu, gpu-interactive, gpu-short and sharing for GPU work. Two you apply for: long and multigpu, once you can show your code uses them well. And two only for courses: courses and courses-gpu.

beats.narration_text: Which one? If you're in a course and have a courses directory, use courses for CPU jobs and courses-gpu for GPU jobs. Otherwise, short for most CPU work; gpu-interactive or gpu-short for interactive GPU sessions; and the gpu partition for GPU batch jobs.

beats.narration_text: A GPU is a processor built for thousands of parallel tasks, and it's what AI and much of modern science run on. To get one interactively, name the partition and the g r e s. Naming the card type gives you exactly that card. Leaving it general gives you whatever is free first, fine for a quick test, but for repeated runs use the same type, or at least record which one you got.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: On the website, an interactive job is a form. For RStudio you pick the version, the partition, the hours, the CPUs and the memory, and press Launch. The defaults are fine to start.

beats.narration_text: The session moves from Queued to Starting to Running, and your time starts when it's running. The card shows the host node, a Cancel button, the time remaining and a session ID. Cancel it when you're done; that frees the node for someone else.

beats.narration_text: The jobs that do most of the real work are batch jobs: set up, submitted, and run without you. Test your commands in an s run session first; then write a script. The S BATCH lines name the job, the partition, one node and sixteen tasks, and ask for email on every event. Then load your software, activate your environment, and run.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Submit it with s batch. Slurm answers with a job ID. When the job runs, its output goes to a file named slurm, dash, the job ID, dot out; cat shows what the job printed. Use less to page through long files, and q to quit. If you're unsure how much to ask for, ask for a little and scale up when a job runs out of memory, CPU or time.
beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Is it running? s queue with your username lists your jobs: ID, partition, name, state, R for running, time and node. s queue for a partition, piped to w c, counts how busy the queue is: five hundred eighteen lines here. And dash dash start estimates when a waiting job will begin.

beats.narration_text: On the website, Jobs, then Active Jobs, shows the same list. And My Interactive Sessions shows each session with its host node and, in parentheses, the seven-digit Slurm job ID you'd give the Research Computing team if something goes wrong.

beats.narration_text: Click the Session ID link and you'll see the files Open OnDemand made for the job. output dot log is the one to read when a session doesn't behave, and the one the team will ask for in a ticket.

beats.narration_text: Now the habit that makes you a power user. Ask for close to the minimum you need, because the more you request, the longer you wait for it. After a job finishes, seff, Slurm efficiency, shows what it actually used. Two real reports from the training. Job one: twelve cores, eight percent CPU efficiency, ten percent of fifty gigabytes used. It could have asked for far less. Job two: eight cores at eighty-four percent CPU efficiency. A much better fit. Try seff on your next finished job.

Act title top-left.

beats.narration_text: Software comes as modules, so you load only what you need, when you need it, because some conflict. module avail lists them; module load loads one, with the exact name and case you saw. Don't put module load in your dot bashrc: it interferes with Open OnDemand and makes your work harder to reproduce.

props.title: ssh — login.explorer.northeastern.edu
lines: # load modules when you need them, not in ~/.bashrc

beats.motion_claim: The real commands and the training's own output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Beyond modules, three routes. Conda environments, which can hold many kinds of scientific software, not only Python. Containers, which the cluster supports. And building from source. And when you're stuck: email r c help at northeastern dot e d u, come to office hours on Zoom, or book a consultation.
beats.motion_claim: Three routes, each landing as one large library icon.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A cluster: you log in to a login node and ask Slurm for a compute node. Two doors: s s h to the login address, or the Open OnDemand website. Home holds seventy-five gigabytes; scratch holds fifty terabytes and is purged monthly; projects is for the long term. s run for a live node, s batch for a script, S queue to check on it. Partitions: short by default, the gpu partitions for GPUs, courses for classes. And seff after every job, so you request close to what you need.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I'm new to a Slurm cluster. Here's what I want to run: [describe your program and data in two sentences]. Tell me which of my files belong in home, scratch and projects; write me an srun command to test it interactively with modest resources; then write the sbatch script for the real run, and tell me which commands I use to check on the job and to read its efficiency afterwards. Then check two things yourself. Does every path it wrote start with a slash? And did it tell you to test with s run before you submit with s batch?
